newsitem.title: FRANCE: French firms create 2nd biggest insurer.
newsitem.headline: French firms create 2nd biggest insurer.

text.p: French insurers Axa and UAP sent a tremor through the industry on Tuesday with the announcement of a mega-merger to create the second largest insurer in the world.

The merger, which in reality looks more like a takeover by Axa of its bigger but less thrusting rival Union des Assurances de Paris, will push German Allianz out of the top spot in Europe and create a group second only to Japan's Nippon Life.

After the merger in mid-1997, the new giant will also be the biggest world player in asset management, with a total turnover across all business areas of 313 billion francs ($62 billion), around 107,000 staff and a stock market capitalisation of 100 billion francs.
"It's the deal of the century for French insurance," said Claude Bebear, chairman of Axa and the one who will head the management board of the new group to be created in mid-1997.

"I have always been convinced that in order survive in the 21st century you absolutely have to have a world-scale business and a size which allows you compete with the big boys," Bebear told reporters.
"Individually we were already among the big boys and now we are the big boy."

Axa is regarded by industry analysts and competitors alike as the quality player in the French insurance sector -- in fact many see it as one of the highest quality and best managed insurers in Europe.
But as one London insurance analyst said on Tuesday: "This deal certainly makes the combined group big, but it remains to be seen whether big will be beautiful."
For Bebear and UAP chairman Jacques Friedmann, who gets the job of head of the new group's supervisory board, there was no doubting that big would be beautiful.
Geographically, Axa would combine prowess in North America and Asia with UAP's dominance in Europe, and notably in Germany through its Colonia unit, they said.
The merger would bring the benefits of economies of scale, a wider product range and more widespread network as well as lower central and asset management costs, they said.
The deal itself involves a complex share swap transaction of four Axa shares plus four certificates -- guaranteeing a minumum price -- for 10 UAP shares.

The "certificates of guaranteed value" offer an important sweetener which ensures UAP shareholders will get the equivalent of 157 francs for each of their shares, a little more than the price of 152 francs per share which small investors paid to buy into UAP when it was privatised in 1994.

While Axa's Bebear said the deal was a "merger", rather than a takeover of UAP, it seemed clear at the news conference that he was indeed in the driving seat as future hands-on boss of the insurance giant-to-be.

Axa, which unlike UAP steered relatively clear of exposure to a collapsed property market, reported a 20 percent jump in net attributable profit in 1995 to 2.73 billion francs and a 51 percent leap in first-half 1996 profit to 1.977 billion francs.

UAP, on the contrary, has been trying to get back into profit after a loss of 2.065 billion francs in 1995, dragged down by provisions of 4.5 billion francs to cover exposure to the moribund property business.
It reported a net attributable profit of 860 million francs for the first six months of 1995 and predicted a return to profit for the year.

French finance minister Jean Arthuis, who must give the nod of approval as well as shareholders, told reporters the merger was a "good project". "Everyone must prepare to be on a European or indeed worldwide scale," he said.
The deal was also welcomed by BNP, which owns 17.2 percent of UAP, and Suez which owns 4.9 percent.
($1=5.057 French Franc)
